title: Foraging hawthorn haws: harvest and uses
subtitle: September to November; discard the seeds
excerpt: Hawthorn produces its deep-red haws from September through November on the thorny shrub that lines UK hedgerows. The flesh is edible and cooks into fruit leather, sauce, and jelly. Discard the seeds; do not crack and eat them.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Crataegus monogyna; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) produces clusters of deep-red haws from September through November on thorny shrubs that line UK hedgerows and scrubland. The flesh is edible and has a dry, apple-like flavour that concentrates well in cooked preparations: fruit leather, sauce, or jelly. Discard the stones inside each haw; do not crack them open to eat the seeds. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
: confirm (1) the round red fruit with one or two hard stones inside, (2) the deeply lobed leaves on the thorny shrub, and (3) the hedgerow, scrubland, or woodland-edge habitat. All three must match.
Fruit: round or oval, deep red, 6 to 12 mm across. One to three hard stones inside. A very small crown of dried sepals at the tip, similar to rosehip but shorter.
Leaves: deeply lobed, three to seven lobes, dark green, 2 to 5 cm long. Very different from rosehip's pinnate leaflets.
Shrub: dense, very thorny, up to 10 m if not trimmed. Produces white five-petalled flowers in May before the leaves are fully out.
Hawthorn is fairly distinctive in its fruiting form. The main UK

to check is yew (Taxus baccata): a red berry-like fruit (an aril, not a true berry) with a single seed, on a dark evergreen tree, not a thorny deciduous shrub. Yew seeds are extremely toxic; the red flesh is not, but there is no safe way to eat around the seed in the field.

Pick from late September through November, after the haws have fully deepened in colour. Strip clusters by hand or use a comb-like motion down the fruiting branch. Wear gloves to protect against the thorns. The haws freeze well before processing; freeze on the day of picking and use within six months.

Rinse in a colander. Simmer in water for 20 to 30 minutes until the flesh is very soft, then push the pulp through a fine-mesh strainer to remove the stones and skin. Use the strained pulp in fruit leather or sauce. For jelly, add the same weight in sugar, simmer until set point, and pour into sterilised jars.

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Leave at least a third of the haws for wildlife; they are a key food source for thrushes and waxwings through winter.

rows.symptom: Haw flesh is mealy and dry even after cooking
rows.cause: The flesh of hawthorn is inherently dry and low in juice
rows.fix: Add more water during simmering and cook longer to soften fully. Hawthorn is better as a puree, leather, or jelly than as a fresh fruit; the dry texture is normal.

rows.symptom: Not sure whether the red fruit is hawthorn or yew
rows.cause: Both produce red fruits in autumn in hedgerow settings
rows.fix: Hawthorn grows on a thorny deciduous shrub with lobed leaves; yew is a non-thorny evergreen tree with flat, dark needles. Do not eat the fruit of yew under any circumstances.
